entries.lesson_title: Windowing a Signal Over a Time Interval
entries.lesson_core_move: Construct a finite-duration version of a continuous-time signal by multiplying it by the shifted-unit-step window $u(t-a)-u(t-b)$ and identifying the interval over which the original signal is retained.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Windowing a Signal Over a Time Interval
sections.learning_goal: Show how a finite-duration signal window is formed as $y(t)=x(t) (u(t-a)-u(t-b))$ and how $a\le b$ creates a retained interval.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No diagrams required; content is expression-first and interval-logic based.

question_policy.practice_question_model: No practice questions for the tutorial section.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Introduce the shifted-unit-step window as a multiplicative gate: it keeps $x(t)$ on an interval and zeroes it elsewhere.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use $x(t)=1$ with $y(t)=1\cdot(u(t)-u(t-b))$ to show the retention interval from $0\le t < b$.
paragraph_plan: Define $u(t)$ and shifted versions $u(t-a)$, $u(t-b)$ as on-off gates.
Show the window product $u(t-a)-u(t-b)$ and state the two switching times $a$ and $b$.
Explain interval retention by reading the step transitions and excluding the region after $t\ge b$.
Connect to familiar 1-line signal construction: multiply any existing $x(t)$ by a window factor.
Add a short sanity check on a generic symbolic expression for $y(t)$.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep terminology exact: "window" means a difference of shifted unit steps. Use closed-open interval phrasing $a\le t<b$ unless boundaries are explicitly altered.

sections.section_title: Windowing a Signal from t=0 to t=b
sections.learning_goal: Construct and interpret the window $u(t)-u(t-b)$ multiplying a base signal from $t=0$ up to $t=b$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; interval and factor are fully specified by formulas.

question_policy.practice_question_model: For $x(t)=t$, form the windowed signal $y(t)=x(t)(u(t)-u(t-b))$ and identify the retained interval.
distractor_plan: Use only $u(t-b)$, missing the leading $u(t)$ and the start edge at 0.
Use $u(t)-u(t+b)$, shifting the cutoff by the wrong sign.
Multiply by $u(t+b)-u(t-b)$, doubling the support interval.
State the retained interval as $0<t\le b$ if the lesson logic assumes right-endpoint inclusion.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Example: Build $y(t)=t\,(u(t)-u(t-b))$ and describe the retained interval and equivalent piecewise form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the result equals $y(t)=t$ on $0\le t < b$ and $y(t)=0$ otherwise.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from a constant base case to a linear base signal, retaining the same start and end of the window.
solution_step_plan: Write the window factor and identify where $u(t)-u(t-b)=1$.
Multiply $x(t)=t$ by the factor and isolate interval conditions.
Express $y(t)$ as a single expression or compact piecewise form with interval bounds.
practice_variation_axes: Change the base signal from $t$ to $At+B$.
Swap endpoint values while preserving lower bound $0$.
Vary sign/zeroing conventions at the boundary only if instructor later specifies them.

sections.handoff_notes: Use boundary language consistently: window is active on $0\le t < b$ for this section unless later corrected.

sections.section_title: Windowing a Signal from t=a to t=b
sections.learning_goal: Construct a shifted finite window $u(t-a)-u(t-b)$ for a base signal and identify retention between arbitrary endpoints.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; shifted interval is signaled directly by $a$ and $b$ in the expression.

question_policy.practice_question_model: For $x(t)=\cos t$, form $y(t)=x(t)(u(t-a)-u(t-b))$ and identify the retention interval in terms of $a$ and $b$.
distractor_plan: Swap the window order to $u(t-b)-u(t-a)$, which inverts the retained interval.
Assume the window includes $t>b$ by using a sum instead of a difference.
Take retention as $a<t\le b$ when the model requires closed-open form.
Misplace subtraction and write $u(t-a)-u(t-b)+u(t)$, adding extra leading support.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Example: For $x(t)=\cos t$, multiply by $u(t-a)-u(t-b)$ and write the exact interval where the cosine component remains.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce a clean statement that the retained part is active for $a\le t < b$ and is zero elsewhere.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Introduces lower bound shift from $0$ to $a$, requiring learners to generalize the same window logic.
solution_step_plan: Substitute $a$ and $b$ into the shifted steps.
Find sign regions of the difference term and mark where it equals 1.
Attach $x(t)$ only on that interval and keep all other regions at 0.
practice_variation_axes: Use an arbitrary base function (polynomial, exponential, trigonometric).
Vary relative order checks with sample parameters $a<b$, and later with concrete numeric anchors.
Introduce parameterized endpoints in model questions while keeping symbolic interval logic.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep expression direction in sync: retained region uses left endpoint $a$ and right endpoint $b$.

sections.section_title: Windowing a Signal Across t=0
sections.learning_goal: Handle windows whose interval crosses the origin and maintain consistent sign/endpoint treatment in $u(t-a)-u(t-b)$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; crossing zero is captured by signed endpoint choices in the formula.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Window $x(t)=e^{-t}$ by $u(t+2)-u(t-3)$. State the final retained interval and which time region remains active.
distractor_plan: Treat both endpoints as positive, giving interval $2\le t<3$ instead of $-2\le t<3$.
Use active interval $-3\le t< -2$ from misreading endpoint signs.
Ignore one step and use only one switch in the factor.
Flip interval polarity by using $u(t-3)-u(t+2)$.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Example: Write the windowed signal $y(t)=e^{-t}(u(t+2)-u(t-3))$ and identify where $y(t)$ is nonzero.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the nonzero interval crosses zero and is correctly reported as $-2\le t<3$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds sign-shifted endpoints that straddle zero, reinforcing parameter interpretation instead of pattern matching to $t=0$ start.
solution_step_plan: Rewrite the two shifted steps and determine when each is 1.
Subtract the activations to find the net window support.
Attach the base signal to that support and keep zero outside the interval.
practice_variation_axes: Swap signs of one endpoint while preserving the other.
Use non-even base signals to prevent symmetry shortcuts.
Test numeric edge cases like adjacent endpoints to avoid reversed intervals.

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize that negative shifts in $u(t-a)$ and $u(t-b)$ move switches left and right on the time axis.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Retained Interval from a Windowed Signal
sections.learning_goal: Given a windowed expression, infer the retained time interval directly from switch times in $u(t-a)-u(t-b)$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No separate image requested; inference is based on symbolic step expression reading.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $y(t)=x(t)(u(t-1)-u(t+4))$, identify the interval where $y(t)$ retains $x(t)$ and select the corrected form.
distractor_plan: Invert the order of endpoints and return interval $-4\le t<1$.
Keep the same expression and conclude support is all $t$, assuming one switch is always redundant.
Use $0\le t<5$ by adding endpoints instead of taking their difference.
Misread $u(t+4)$ as switching on at $t=4$ instead of at $t=-4$.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Example: From $y(t)=x(t)(u(t-2)-u(t-5))$, identify the window interval and rewrite a clean retained-domain sentence.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Report the active interval for $x(t)$ and verify that the expression matches a single contiguous finite window.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Reverses from constructing the window to reading it from a finished formula, testing inverse skill.
solution_step_plan: Locate the two switching terms and sort the two times.
Determine where the difference of steps equals one.
Translate that condition to retained interval notation used by the course.
practice_variation_axes: Vary coefficient signs and parameter positions $u(t-a)-u(t-b)$.
Check interpretation when $a<b$ and when $a>b$ as an error-spotting case.
Ask for both interval statement and equivalent piecewise support conditions.

sections.handoff_notes: For quality, ensure question bank covers both correct-interpretation and failure cases where $a>b$ is not physically valid.

entries.lesson_core_move: Construct a piecewise constant continuous-time signal by converting its interval-by-interval level changes into a sum of scaled shifted unit steps.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Building Piecewise Constant Signals
sections.learning_goal: Interpret a piecewise constant signal as a baseline level plus a sequence of level changes driven by shifted unit steps.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visuals required for this section.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that each piecewise constant jump is represented by a shifted unit step scaled by that jump size.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Introduce the base form for one transition from 0 to a nonzero level using one term $A u(t-a)$.
paragraph_plan: State the objective: represent interval-by-interval constants with sums of shifted unit steps.
Define what a unit step does to a signal and identify left/right regions.
Work a symbolic one-step-on example and verify region values.
Extend to a finite window by subtracting a second step.
Transition to nonzero-to-nonzero transitions and then multiple transitions.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Not used for tutorial sections.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Not used for tutorial sections.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Not used for tutorial sections.
solution_step_plan: Introduce base-case explanation and defer worked-example output generation to section 2.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section tightly scoped and symbolic to reduce extraneous cognitive load before the first example.

sections.section_title: Turning On a Constant Level with a Shifted Unit Step
sections.learning_goal: Construct a nonzero constant after a start time using a single shifted unit step term.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: Pure symbolic task; no figures required.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Write the unit-step form for $x(t)=0$ for $t<2$ and $x(t)=5$ for $t\ge2$.
distractor_plan: Use $5u(t)$ instead of $5u(t-2)$.
Drop the scale coefficient and write just $u(t-2)$.
Move the amplitude to a negative sign, e.g., $-5u(t-2)$.
Use $u(2-t)$ instead of $u(t-2)$.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Guide example construction from interval statement to one shifted-step expression and interval check.
paragraph_plan: Start from the start time and baseline.
Map interval statement to $A u(t-a)$ form.
Verify output at left and right regions.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Write a unit-step form for the signal $y(t)=0$ for $t<2$, and $y(t)=5$ for $t\ge2$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce the one-term step representation and show it matches the two regions.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: First worked example that applies the tutorial base-case directly with one shifted step.
solution_step_plan: Read start time and amplitude from the interval definition.
Choose form $A u(t-a)$.
Check left region gives 0 and right region gives 5.

sections.handoff_notes: Practice can reuse this motif with different values of $A$ and $a$.

sections.section_title: Turning Off a Constant Level with a Second Shifted Unit Step
sections.learning_goal: Create a finite nonzero interval using a positive step to turn on and a second shifted step to turn it off.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep algebraic only to support jump-form fluency.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Build the expression for $x(t)=4$ on $1\le t<5$ and $x(t)=0$ otherwise.
distractor_plan: Use only one step term and miss finite support.
Swap onset and offset order.
Use wrong signs for the subtraction term.
Use identical amplitudes but incorrect breakpoints.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show finite support as the difference of two shifted steps.
paragraph_plan: Write the activate term at first breakpoint.
Write the deactivate term at second breakpoint with negative sign.
Combine and verify interval behavior.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Construct a unit-step equation for $x(t)=4$ when $1\le t<5$, and $x(t)=0$ elsewhere.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce a finite pulse expression and verify it is 0 before and after the interval.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds a second breakpoint and introduces subtraction to remove activity after the second shift.
solution_step_plan: Identify interval start and end times.
Write activation term $4u(t-1)$.
Write turn-off term $-4u(t-5)$.
Combine and evaluate piecewise to validate all regions.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep distractors close to correct form so question generator can mirror small arithmetic/sign mistakes.

sections.section_title: Changing Directly Between Two Nonzero Constant Levels
sections.learning_goal: Represent transitions between two nonzero levels through cumulative jump increments rather than zero reset.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No diagram needed; focus on signed jump computations.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Convert $x(t)=2$ for $t<1$, $x(t)=5$ for $1\le t<3$, and $x(t)=2$ for $t\ge3$ into step form.
distractor_plan: Use wrong jump size at the second transition.
Use baseline 0 instead of baseline 2.
Swap jump values as if the second transition returned to 0.
Mis-order the breakpoints in the expression.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Model a direct level-to-level jump with baseline-plus-$\Delta$ terms.
paragraph_plan: State baseline and list each level change.
Compute each jump from the prior level.
Assemble compact signed sum with shifted steps.
Confirm interval values using piecewise evaluation.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Convert the piecewise signal $x(t)=2$ for $t<1$, $x(t)=5$ for $1\le t<3$, and $x(t)=2$ for $t\ge3$ to unit-step form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Create a compact sum of jump terms and verify nonzero-to-nonzero transitions.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extends finite-window pattern to transitions between nonzero levels using positive and negative deltas.
solution_step_plan: Set baseline $y_0=2$.
Compute $\delta$ at $t=1$: $\Delta A_1=5-2=3$.
Compute $\delta$ at $t=3$: $\Delta A_2=2-5=-3$.
Check each interval and edge cases.

sections.handoff_notes: Reinforce the rule that each new breakpoint contributes only one signed jump equal to new level minus prior level.

sections.section_title: Combining Multiple Level Changes into One Step Expression
sections.learning_goal: Build and simplify a multi-breakpoint piecewise constant signal by summing baseline and several jump amplitudes.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed for this symbolic synthesis step.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Convert $x(t)=1$ for $t<0$, $x(t)=4$ for $0\le t<2$, $x(t)=-2$ for $2\le t<4$, and $x(t)=3$ for $t\ge4$ into a single expression.
distractor_plan: Compute jumps from original level instead of prior-level increments.
Use only two transitions instead of three.
Place breakpoint times in the wrong order.
Drop the initial baseline term and shift all deltas incorrectly.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Demonstrate scaling pattern to several transitions while preserving a single summation-style structure.
paragraph_plan: List intervals in order with level values.
Convert each breakpoint into one jump term.
Sum baseline and jumps into compact form.
Optionally simplify by grouping like terms where useful.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Write one unit-step expression for $x(t)=1$ if $t<0$, $x(t)=4$ if $0\le t<2$, $x(t)=-2$ if $2\le t<4$, and $x(t)=3$ if $t\ge4$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate multi-breakpoint construction and verify all interval values in a single compact expression.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds cumulative complexity by combining several positive and negative jump terms in one expression.
solution_step_plan: Set baseline level $y_0=1$.
Compute $\Delta A_1=4-1=3$ at $t=0$.
Compute $\Delta A_2=-2-4=-6$ at $t=2$.
Compute $\Delta A_3=3-(-2)=5$ at $t=4$.
Check each interval from $t<0$ to $t\ge4$.

sections.handoff_notes: Use this section as the general template for later topics: baseline plus ordered $\delta$ terms and direct interval verification.

entries.lesson_core_move: Construct a piecewise linear continuous-time signal by converting each breakpoint's slope change into a shifted ramp term gated by unit steps.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Building Piecewise Linear Signals
sections.learning_goal: Explain how each slope change in a piecewise linear continuous-time signal maps to a shifted ramp term, then show how multiple shifted ramps combine into one expression.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed because the step is driven by algebraic ramp identities.

question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable
distractor_plan: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the core identity that a slope segment can be written as a shifted ramp coefficient: $\Delta m\,r(t-a)=\Delta m(t-a)u(t-a)$, and that active slope at any time is the sum of active increments from these terms.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start from one base ramp: $x(t)=m\,r(t-a)=m(t-a)u(t-a)$ and read its behavior piecewise.
paragraph_plan: State the goal of representing piecewise linear signals with shifted ramp blocks instead of full case-by-case pieces.
Define $r(t-a)$ and show how $u(t-a)$ gates the slope contribution.
Show one-line slope accumulation across time by adding ramp terms with breakpoint offsets.
Demonstrate interval-limited segments with ramp differences, e.g. $r(t-a)-r(t-b)$.
Preview example progression: one shifted ramp, one breakpoint increment, finite-interval slope, then multiple increments.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: not-applicable
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: not-applicable
example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable
solution_step_plan: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: Keep notation consistent with module notation for shifted unit steps and ramp terms; use only symbolic expressions and avoid graph dependence.

sections.section_title: Starting a Signal with One Shifted Ramp
sections.learning_goal: Build one-piece piecewise linear signals by starting the slope with a single shifted ramp.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No graph data is required for this symbolic start-form step.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Write an expression for the signal that is $0$ for $t<-1$ and equals $2(t+1)$ for $t\ge -1$.
distractor_plan: Incorrect shift direction such as $2(t+1)u(t)$.
Miss the ramp form and use $2u(t+1)$ instead.
Use $2(t-1)u(t+1)$ with an inconsistent time shift.
Add an extra constant offset not implied by the target function.
Omit unit-step gating and return $2(t+1)$ for all $t$.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Express $x(t)$ where $x(t)=0$ for $t<-1$ and $x(t)=2(t+1)$ for $t\ge -1$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce $x(t)=2\,r(t+1)$ and confirm that this equals $2(t+1)$ only after the gate opens.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extends the introduced base form to a delayed/advanced start time example.
solution_step_plan: Identify that the target starts at $t=-1$ with slope 2.
Form the shifted ramp $r(t+1)=(t+1)u(t+1)$.
Scale by 2 to get $2r(t+1)$.
Check values for $t<-1$ and $t\ge-1$ to verify piecewise behavior.
practice_variation_axes: Shift time to different activation point

sections.handoff_notes: The example should anchor the student's interpretation of $r(t-a)$ as a time-late linear segment creator.

sections.section_title: Adding a Slope Change at a Breakpoint
sections.learning_goal: Represent one interior breakpoint where slope increases or decreases by adding a shifted ramp increment.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: Symbolic slope-difference control is the key artifact here.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Choose the expression for slope 1 from $t=0$ and slope 4 after $t=3$, with zero output before $t=0$.
distractor_plan: Use only one term $r(t)$ and miss the breakpoint increment.
Apply increment at wrong time $t=2$ or $t=4$.
Use a unit-step constant $3u(t-3)$ instead of ramp increment.
Subtract the increment instead of adding it.
Omit the starting baseline slope and use only $3r(t-3)$.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Express a signal that has slope 0 for $t<0$, slope 1 on $[0,3)$, and slope 4 for $t\ge3$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Build and interpret the representation $x(t)=r(t)+3r(t-3)$ to show slope jump of $+3$ at $t=3$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from a single ramp activation to a sustained breakpoint slope change.
solution_step_plan: Set the initial slope segment as $r(t)$.
Compute slope change at $t=3$ as $\Delta m=3$.
Add the increment term $3r(t-3)$.
Check slope in each interval by reading ramp derivatives.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep students focused on slope increments, not value continuity at breakpoints.

sections.section_title: Returning the Slope to Zero After an Interval
sections.learning_goal: Terminate slope activity after a time interval by adding a second shifted ramp term with opposite coefficient.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual is needed; interval-limited slope is an algebraic difference-of-ramps pattern.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Find the step expression for slope 2 on $[0,2)$ and slope 0 for $t\ge2$.
distractor_plan: Use only $2r(t)$, which keeps slope active forever.
Use $2r(t-2)$ as the only term, losing the segment start.
Use subtraction without a delayed difference, e.g., $2r(t)-2$.
Reverse terms as $2r(t-2)-2r(t)$.
Use gate sign $u(2-t)$ instead of $u(t-2)$.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Construct $x(t)=2t$ for $0\le t<2$ and constant for $t\ge2$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Derive $x(t)=2r(t)-2r(t-2)$ and verify constant continuation after $t=2$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds a cancellation term that turns a permanent slope into a finite interval slope.
solution_step_plan: Start from active slope term $2r(t)$.
Introduce stop term $2r(t-2)$.
Subtract the stop term: $2r(t)-2r(t-2)$.
Check function value at $t=1$ and $t=3$ to verify behavior.

sections.handoff_notes: This pattern is the core reusable template for finite-duration linear pieces in later triangular constructions.

sections.section_title: Combining Multiple Slope Changes in One Expression
sections.learning_goal: Combine several breakpoint slope changes into a single compact unit-step ramp expression.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No images should be required because the step compounds deterministic algebraic terms.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Choose the expression for slopes $[0,1,4,2]$ on breakpoints $t=0,2,5$ with zero initial value.
distractor_plan: Skip one breakpoint term and collapse two intervals.
Use only constants with $u(t-a)$ instead of ramp differences.
Use wrong slope increment signs causing opposite slope direction.
Anchor all terms at incorrect start times.
Add extra offset terms that change the piecewise values.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Represent a signal with slope profile: 0 for $t<0$, 1 for $0\le t<2$, 4 for $2\le t<5$, and 2 for $t\ge5$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Build the compact form using baseline slope and increment/decrement terms with shifted ramps.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extends from one breakpoint to chained breakpoints and mixed slope changes.
solution_step_plan: Write baseline slope after first active time.
Add an increment term at each breakpoint for slope change.
Use interval-ending correction at the next breakpoint where needed.
Assemble terms in one line and verify slopes in each interval.
practice_variation_axes: Sign and size of each slope increment

sections.handoff_notes: Keep term ordering explicit by ascending breakpoints and consistent use of $r(t-a)-r(t-b)$ for interval bounds.

entries.lesson_core_move: Construct a finite-duration triangular signal from its rise, peak, fall, and zero regions using shifted linear segments gated by unit steps.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Building Triangular Signals
sections.learning_goal: Identify a finite-duration triangle as three regions (rise, peak boundary, fall) and map each region to one gated linear term.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show the triangle decomposition pattern $x(t)=\text{rise segment}+\text{fall segment}$, then gate each segment with step differences so the signal is nonzero only on the active interval.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use the unit-height unit-width base triangle: rise on $[0,1]$, peak at $t=1$, fall on $[1,2]$.
paragraph_plan: State the interval structure for piecewise triangles: zero before $t_0$, rising linear on $[t_0,t_p)$, falling linear on $[t_p,t_1)$, and zero after $t_1$.
Define a generic slope form for each linear region and encode each region using $u(t-a)-u(t-b)$ as a window.
Show one worked algebraic form that combines both regions in one expression and enforces continuity at $t_p$.
Summarize the target check list: window boundaries, endpoint values, and value at the peak.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep tutorial strict: no question planning, no final answer key, and no image dependency. Emphasize the shift-window template only once, then let the example steps apply it.

sections.section_title: Building a Basic Triangle from Rising and Falling Segments
sections.learning_goal: Convert a simple symmetric unit-height triangle into one step-based expression with separate rising and falling linear windows.

question_policy.answer_format: five symbolic expression options with exactly one correct
question_policy.practice_question_model: Write a step-function expression for a unit-height triangle that rises linearly from $0$ at $t=0$ to $1$ at $t=1$ and falls back to $0$ at $t=2$.
distractor_plan: Use one step term for the whole triangle instead of two windows.
Swap the rise and fall windows or shift boundaries by one unit.
Keep the right slope sign but include the wrong intercept in the fall segment.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find a unit-step representation for the triangle $x(t)$ with $x(t)=0$ for $t<0$ and $t>2$, $x(t)=t$ on $0\le t<1$, and $x(t)=2-t$ on $1\le t<2$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Derive and combine the two gated linear pieces into $x(t)=t(u(t)-u(t-1))+(-t+2)(u(t-1)-u(t-2))$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first full worked example that applies the tutorial template to concrete endpoint times and slopes.
solution_step_plan: List the active intervals and confirm the rise/fall formulas on each interval.
Write rise term as $t(u(t)-u(t-1))$.
Write fall term as $(-t+2)(u(t-1)-u(t-2))$.
Sum terms and verify continuity at $t=1$, zero output outside $[0,2]$, and peak height $1$.
practice_variation_axes: Change interval endpoints while preserving linear rise/fall.
Replace unit peak height with a variable height parameter in one segment.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep both terms gated by adjacent step differences and do not simplify into a single polynomial over all t.

sections.section_title: Building a Shifted Triangle from Start, Peak, and End Times
sections.learning_goal: Generalize the base triangle to arbitrary start, peak, and end times using shifted linear formulas inside the same step-window structure.

question_policy.answer_format: five symbolic expressions with one mathematically correct choice
question_policy.practice_question_model: Write a step-form expression for a triangle that starts at $t=2$, peaks at height $3$ at $t=5$, and ends at $t=8$.
distractor_plan: Use windowing intervals based on $[2,5]$ and $[5,8]$ but apply wrong slope magnitudes.
Reverse rise/fall terms while keeping peak height unchanged.
Use only one window difference and miss one of the breakpoints.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Construct the step-form expression for $x(t)$ where $x(t)=\frac{1}{3}(t-2)$ on $[2,5)$, and $x(t)=-\frac{3}{2}t+\frac{15}{2}$ on $[5,8)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how to translate shifted start/peak/end times into gating pairs $u(t-a)-u(t-b)$ and assemble the full triangle.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds a time shift and nontrivial slopes, requiring explicit conversion of $a,p,b$ into two separate ramp windows.
solution_step_plan: Compute rise slope from $(t,p,x)=(2,5,3)$ and write the rise formula on $[2,5)$.
Compute fall formula through points $(5,3)$ and $(8,0)$.
Gate each formula with $u(t-2)-u(t-5)$ and $u(t-5)-u(t-8)$ respectively.
Combine and verify the two-window form is continuous and zero outside $[2,8]$.
practice_variation_axes: Move all three key times $(a,p,b)$ while preserving ordering.
Vary peak height while keeping $a,p,b$ fixed.
Use equivalent slope-intercept forms in either segment.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep formulas in $(a,p,b)$-style parameters for reuse, then specialize in practice; avoid introducing new transform identities.

sections.section_title: Building a Nonunit-Height Triangular Signal
sections.learning_goal: Scale the core rise/fall template to arbitrary peak height while preserving window boundaries and continuity at the peak.

question_policy.answer_format: five symbolic expression options with one mathematically correct response
question_policy.practice_question_model: Write the step expression for a triangle that starts at $t=0$, peaks at height $4$ at $t=2$, and returns to zero at $t=4$.
distractor_plan: Use unit peak height in one of the gated terms.
Drop the peak-continuity condition and let the two pieces disagree at $t_p$.
Misplace the step boundary offsets, causing a gap or overlap in active intervals.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find a step-form model for $x(t)$ with $x(t)=2t$ on $0\le t<2$, $x(t)=8-2t$ on $2\le t<4$, and $x(t)=0$ otherwise.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Apply the same two-window structure while adjusting amplitudes to peak height $4$ and keeping continuity at $t=2$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Introduces nonunit peak height and checks that amplitude scaling is embedded inside both rise and fall formulas.
solution_step_plan: Set rise formula on $[0,2)$ as $2t(u(t)-u(t-2))$.
Set fall formula on $[2,4)$ as $(8-2t)(u(t-2)-u(t-4))$.
Sum terms and simplify only if needed for presentation.
Verify value at $t=0,2,4$ and confirm zero output outside interval.
practice_variation_axes: Change peak height while keeping $0\le t \le 4$ support.
Shift support interval and keep the same peak height.
Use different but equivalent slope-intercept representations.

sections.handoff_notes: Prefer explicit arithmetic in worked example so later question generators can mirror by swapping coefficients and interval endpoints.

sections.section_title: Building an Asymmetric Triangular Signal with Unequal Slopes
sections.learning_goal: Construct asymmetric triangles by assigning different rise and fall slopes while keeping gating boundaries and continuity constraints explicit.

question_policy.answer_format: five symbolic expression choices; one correct algebraic construction
question_policy.practice_question_model: Build the step form for a triangle with rise on $[0,1]$ to height $2$ and fall on $[1,4]$ back to zero.
distractor_plan: Set rise and fall slopes to the same value, making the signal symmetric.
Use $u(t)-u(t-1)$ for both terms so the fall term never turns on.
Keep the peak at $t=4$ by mistake rather than $t=1$.
Write fall line as $2t+...$ with the wrong sign.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find a step-function expression for $x(t)=2t$ on $0\le t<1$, $x(t)=\frac{8-2t}{3}$ on $1\le t<4$, and $x(t)=0$ otherwise.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Create a valid representation with unequal slopes by computing each slope separately and preserving the same step-window pattern.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds slope asymmetry; rise and fall coefficients differ and are no longer mirror images.
solution_step_plan: Write separate rise and fall linear expressions from the given endpoint conditions.
Attach $u(t)-u(t-1)$ to the rise region and $u(t-1)-u(t-4)$ to the fall region.
Sum the pieces and verify continuity at $t=1$ and zero output outside $[0,4]$.
Check peak value at the breakpoint to confirm asymmetric slope handling.
practice_variation_axes: Vary rise time and fall time independently while preserving peak time and height.
Shift all breakpoints by a constant delay.
Change peak height while maintaining unequal slopes.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep region boundaries explicit to avoid sign/order errors that commonly cause discontinuities at the peak.

entries.lesson_core_move: Simplify overlapping shifted-unit-step expressions by identifying their active time intervals and combining like signal segments into an equivalent compact expression.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Simplifying Step-Function Expressions
sections.learning_goal: Anchor the student in a concrete workflow: convert an overlapping step expression into piecewise active intervals, add active coefficients, then rewrite the result as a compact equivalent expression.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image is needed; this step is purely symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use a symbolic walkthrough with interval notation and coefficient bookkeeping only.

question_policy.practice_question_model: No practice questions in the tutorial step.
distractor_plan: No distractors for a non-question tutorial section.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the learner to simplify an expression like $2u(t-1)-u(t-2)+3u(t-3)$ by identifying interval boundaries from shifted steps, summing active amplitudes in each interval, and expressing the reduced result as non-overlapping step terms.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start from two-step overlap only, e.g., $u(t)-u(t-1) + u(t-1)$, then collapse the active value on the shared boundary regions.
paragraph_plan: Introduce the active-interval view of a shifted-step term and identify each term's switch time as a candidate boundary.
Demonstrate a sorted-boundary checklist on a single overlap example and map each interval to the subset of active step terms.
Show coefficient accumulation in each interval, including cancellation where positive and negative segments overlap.
Show how to write the simplified piecewise form from interval values and convert it back to a compact step expression if needed.
Summarize a repeatable sequence: find boundaries, sort intervals, combine active coefficients, simplify by interval, then emit compact output.
display_math_plan: $$\text{Step boundaries: }t=1,2\;\Rightarrow\; \text{active interval values are computed piecewise}$$

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Not applicable for tutorial sections.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: No worked example is needed in this tutorial step.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: No variation step needed for the tutorial step.
solution_step_plan: No worked example is provided in the tutorial section.
practice_variation_axes: No practice questions in tutorial section.

sections.handoff_notes: Use this section to establish the exact sequence and notation for all subsequent examples. Keep it compact and symbol-focused so cognitive load stays low.

sections.section_title: Identifying Active Intervals in Shifted Unit Step Expressions
sections.learning_goal: Compute active intervals for a shifted-step expression and write its interval values correctly before simplification.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; interval boundaries and symbols are sufficient.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not include plots; use boundary tables and piecewise notation only.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $x(t)=2u(t-1)-3u(t-4)+u(t-5)$, identify the interval-value expression between breakpoints.
distractor_plan: Include distractors that miss a boundary point.
Include distractors that keep a step active in the wrong interval.
Include distractors that accidentally reorder boundaries.
Include distractors that confuse strict versus non-strict switching at $t=a$.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find the active intervals for $x(t)=3u(t-1)-u(t-3)+2u(t-5)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Create the boundary set $\{1,3,5\}$, evaluate active subsets on each interval, and produce the interval-value expression before combining terms.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Builds directly on the tutorial by removing the generic two-term prototype and adding a third boundary and mixed coefficients.
solution_step_plan: List switch times from each factor as $t=1,3,5$.
Sort boundaries and split line into $t<1$, $1\le t<3$, $3\le t<5$, $t\ge5$.
For each region, include terms with active arguments (nonzero coefficients) and sum amplitudes.
Record the piecewise active value map and keep it for simplification conversion.
practice_variation_axes: Add or remove one extra shifted term.

sections.handoff_notes: This example should train interval book-keeping. Keep worked example and questions consistent on interval partitioning only, with no picture dependency.

sections.section_title: Combining Overlapping Constant Step Terms
sections.learning_goal: Convert overlapping constant-amplitude step terms into a compact equivalent expression by combining interval sums.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; use a compact algebraic interval table.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: If needed, provide a sorted interval table textually, not as a diagram.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Simplify $x(t)=2u(t-1)-u(t-2)+u(t-4)-u(t-5)$ into an equivalent compact form.
distractor_plan: One distractor should skip combining overlaps in one interval.
One distractor should keep an inactive term active too long.
One distractor should preserve boundaries but with incorrect coefficients.
One distractor should reverse a subtraction sign before reassembly.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Simplify $x(t)=u(t-2)+2u(t-4)-3u(t-6)$ and write a compact equivalent expression.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Derive interval values, combine constant coefficients on each interval, and rewrite with the shortest correct difference-of-steps form.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This adds direct coefficient accumulation and elimination of redundant intermediate levels for the first time.
solution_step_plan: Compute interval boundaries $2,4,6$ and evaluate the net value per interval.
Merge consecutive intervals with equal net value when possible, if permitted by boundaries.
Translate the reduced piecewise map back into one compact step expression with updated coefficients.
Check that each merged interval has matching activation/deactivation steps.
practice_variation_axes: Change signs to force both positive and negative cancellations.
Test whether learners merge equal-valued adjacent intervals correctly.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this step focused on constant terms only; this avoids slope-handling complexity and preserves progression from prior interval logic.

sections.section_title: Combining Overlapping Sloped Step Terms
sections.learning_goal: Extend overlap simplification to shifted linear terms where active interval coefficients are linear functions of $t$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; use symbolic linear forms and interval checks.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not include graph-dependent representations.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Simplify $x(t)=(t-1)u(t-1)-2(t-3)u(t-3)+u(t-5)$ using interval simplification.
distractor_plan: One distractor should correctly find intervals but fail to combine slopes in one region.
One distractor should drop the shift in one linear factor.
One distractor should keep an early slope term active too far into later intervals.
One distractor should mishandle the intercept created by overlap.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Simplify $x(t)=(t-2)u(t-2)-(t-4)u(t-4)$ and express it as a compact piecewise form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Track active slopes in each interval, simplify algebraically within each region, then reconstruct the compact result.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds one level of complexity by replacing constant coefficients with sloped expressions while preserving the same interval workflow.
solution_step_plan: Write switch times and interval list from shifted arguments.
Substitute active terms in each interval and expand/simplify linear pieces.
Look for equal neighboring piecewise segments to remove redundant step flips if valid.
Optionally compress to equivalent step form and preserve domain boundaries.
Verify continuity and endpoint behavior at each breakpoint.
practice_variation_axes: Shift all slopes by different times.
Add a third overlapping sloped term with a different slope.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the worked example explicit that slopes are evaluated only in active intervals, never globally.

sections.section_title: Rewriting Redundant Step Terms into Compact Expressions
sections.learning_goal: Eliminate redundant or canceling step terms and produce a cleaner, equivalent expression in minimal overlap form.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; use symbolic cancellation checks only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use algebraic difference-of-step identities when available to simplify structure.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Rewrite $x(t)=u(t-1)-2u(t-3)+2u(t-3)-u(t-5)$ into the most compact equivalent step form.
distractor_plan: Include distractor that leaves opposite-sign paired terms uncanceled.
Include distractor that removes terms but introduces incorrect new switch points.
Include distractor that simplifies magnitude but wrongs signs.
Include distractor that compresses to fewer terms but changes active interval order.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Rewrite $x(t)=u(t-2)-u(t-4)+u(t-4)-u(t-6)$ as a compact equivalent expression.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Detect and remove redundant neighbors, keep only net-effective switch events, and verify equivalence interval by interval.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Uses the same interval mechanism but introduces cancellation and elimination of adjacent redundant terms.
solution_step_plan: Compute boundary set and evaluate interval map.
Cancel coefficients that net to zero in shared subintervals.
Rewrite the result with fewer step terms by removing inactive or canceling boundaries.
Check equivalence by sampling one test $t$ from each resulting interval.

sections.handoff_notes: This is the bridge into compactness quality. Keep the focus on proof by interval equivalence, not visual intuition.

sections.section_title: Checking Simplified Step Expressions by Time Interval
sections.learning_goal: Validate a simplified form by sampling canonical intervals and confirming exact equality with original segment logic.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; use symbolic interval test points and tables.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Only symbolic verification artifacts are required.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Check whether the proposed simplification $y(t)=u(t-1)-u(t-4)$ matches $x(t)=u(t-1)-u(t-2)+u(t-2)-u(t-4)$ by interval testing.
distractor_plan: One distractor should pass only on one interval and fail others.
One distractor should test endpoint only and miss interior mismatch.
One distractor should confuse strict vs. non-strict activation at a switch point.
One distractor should show algebraic equivalence on paper but incorrect boundary conditions.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Verify that $x(t)=2u(t-1)-u(t-3)-u(t-5)+u(t-4)$ is equivalent to a candidate compact form by checking each active interval.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Confirm equivalence by evaluating original and candidate on each interval representative, and confirm no interval mismatch at boundaries.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Shifts from rewriting to verification, enforcing error-checking as the final lesson-step skill.
solution_step_plan: Compute canonical boundary times from both forms.
Pick representative sample times in every interval.
Evaluate both forms numerically or symbolically at each sample and compare.
If mismatch appears, identify the smallest fix in interval map and restate corrected compact form.
practice_variation_axes: Include candidates with one missing or one extra switch.
Vary boundary ordering and candidate complexity.
Add distractor candidates that differ only on a single interval.

sections.handoff_notes: End lesson with verification skill transfer: every simplification should pass an interval equality check before release to the question stage.

entries.lesson_title: Converting Graphs into Unit Step Expressions
entries.lesson_core_move: Translate a continuous-time signal graph into a simplified unit step expression by identifying its breakpoints, interval formulas, and shifted unit-step windows.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Converting Graphs into Unit Step Expressions
sections.learning_goal: Establish the minimum set of graph-reading actions needed to rewrite a signal graph as a sum of shifted unit-step windows.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A clean continuous-time graph with labeled time axis, a single nonzero interval, and highlighted breakpoints a and b.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use clean axes, high contrast strokes, and only essential labels for breakpoints and segment value.

question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Introduce the conversion pipeline: read all breakpoints from the graph, map each active interval to a difference of two shifted steps, and attach the interval formula to each gated term.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use one pulse example with $x(t)=A$ on $0\le t<T$ and $x(t)=0$ elsewhere to show $x(t)=A\,\big(u(t)-u(t-T)\big)$.
paragraph_plan: Define graph-to-window translation and why interval boundaries are the main objects to identify.
Introduce the base rule for a finite interval using two shifted unit steps.
Explain how segment formulas multiply the window term.
Preview the sequence: first parse intervals, then convert single segments, then combine and simplify.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: N/A for tutorial section.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: N/A for tutorial section.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: N/A for tutorial section.
solution_step_plan: N/A for tutorial section.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section tightly focused on the core conversion method so students build a stable schema before solving any example conversions.

sections.section_title: Identifying Breakpoints and Interval Formulas from a Graph
sections.learning_goal: Given a graph, extract an ordered breakpoint list and corresponding interval formulas before writing step terms.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A graph with alternating zero and nonzero pieces, including negative and positive breakpoints and piecewise values.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use the same visual style as the tutorial image so learners transfer the parsing routine directly.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Given this graph, choose the correct ordered list of breakpoints and interval formulas.
distractor_plan: Swap adjacent breakpoints and change interval order.
Use only every other interval and collapse others.
Ignore continuity conventions at endpoint transitions.
Misread negative-time segments as all positive-time.
Omit one interval that returns to zero

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Read the displayed graph and write the interval formula table $\{(t_0,t_1]: f_1,\ (t_1,t_2]:f_2,\dots\}$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce a complete, ordered interval map that preserves values and boundaries for future conversion.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extends the base case by handling multiple nonzero zones and negative-time regions.
solution_step_plan: Mark every breakpoint in increasing time order.
Assign the graph value formula to each open interval between neighboring breakpoints.
Check endpoint handling at each breakpoint and note if value is included or excluded.
Return the interval table as ordered data for conversion.
practice_variation_axes: Mixtures of zero and nonzero intervals

sections.handoff_notes: This section is data extraction only; avoid introducing step algebra yet.

sections.section_title: Converting a Single Nonzero Graph Segment into a Step Window Term
sections.learning_goal: Convert one isolated nonzero interval into the canonical shifted-window form $A(u(t-a)-u(t-b))$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Graph with one isolated nonzero segment: $x(t)=A$ on $a\le t < b$, zero elsewhere.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Show only one active segment so the gate-rule $u(t-a)-u(t-b)$ is unmistakable.

question_policy.practice_question_model: From the graph, select the correct single-window conversion expression.
distractor_plan: Reverse step order to $u(t-b)-u(t-a)$.
Use only one step $A u(t-a)$.
Shift both breakpoints by the wrong sign.
Drop amplitude and write unit height.
Use $u(t-b)-u(t-a)$ with the same symbols.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Convert the graph with $x(t)=A$ for $a\le t<b$ and $x(t)=0$ elsewhere into a step form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Create the exact gated expression and verify it turns on at $t=a$ and off at $t=b$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This adds conversion of a concrete isolated segment after interval extraction.
solution_step_plan: Read interval endpoints $a$ and $b$ from the graph.
Write base gate $u(t-a)-u(t-b)$.
Multiply gate by segment amplitude $A$.
Test representative times outside and inside the interval.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this as a single-term conversion so learners trust the window-difference template.

sections.section_title: Converting a Piecewise Constant Graph into Shifted Unit Steps
sections.learning_goal: Translate multiple constant pieces into a signed sum of shifted unit-step window terms.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Graph with two or more nonzero constant plateaus at different heights and at least one negative value.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Render jumps distinctly so each change in level is obvious without extra annotations.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Choose the unit-step expression that matches the piecewise constant graph with multiple level changes.
distractor_plan: Drop or merge separate intervals into one wide interval.
Assign the wrong sign for descending levels.
Use incorrect order of window endpoints.
Combine all nonzero sections into a single coefficient.
Omit one transition segment in the sum.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Convert the graph $0\to A\to B\to 0$ over two intervals to a unit-step sum.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce one shifted-window term per nonzero plateau and combine signs correctly.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds independent terms for multiple constant intervals beyond the single-segment case.
solution_step_plan: List all nonzero constant intervals and their heights.
Write one window term for each interval.
Scale each gate by its interval amplitude.
Sum terms and inspect interval-wise values.

sections.handoff_notes: This is the core multi-term assembly pattern used for most piecewise-constant graphs.

sections.section_title: Converting a Piecewise Linear Graph into Windowed Segment Formulas
sections.learning_goal: Translate linear ramps in a graph into windowed segment formulas and combine with constant windows as needed.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Piecewise linear graph with one rising segment and one falling segment between labeled breakpoints.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep slopes as integer or simple fractional values for readability and consistent gating checks.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Select the correct windowed linear expression for this graph with rise and fall sections.
distractor_plan: Use a constant window for a segment that is linear.
Flip slope sign in one segment.
Misplace the start or stop shift.
Skip gating on/off and let ramp continue indefinitely.
Use an incorrect baseline in the linear formula.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Convert a graph with one linear rise and one linear fall into a sum of windowed ramp formulas.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Generate a correct expression that activates each ramp only on its intended interval.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds nonconstant segment structure after constant-piece conversion.
solution_step_plan: Identify each linear segment’s slope and intercept form.
Attach each segment with start and end windows.
Sum all piece terms and check continuity at breakpoints.
Simplify where adjacent windows share shift structure.
practice_variation_axes: Sign change between rise and fall

sections.handoff_notes: Avoid introducing notation beyond ramp-window forms already introduced in previous module lessons.

sections.section_title: Writing a Simplified Unit Step Expression from a Multi-Segment Graph
sections.learning_goal: Assemble and simplify the full unit-step expression for a graph with mixed constant and linear segments.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Graph with several mixed constant and linear segments, including at least one negative amplitude and multiple breakpoints.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the same scale and line conventions as earlier sections for direct consistency checks.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Choose the most simplified unit-step expression equivalent to the full multi-segment graph.
distractor_plan: Keep redundant overlapping terms unsimplified.
Incorrectly merge nonadjacent intervals.
Attach wrong amplitude to one segment.
Misplace window endpoints after simplification.
Lose continuity by missing one breakpoint term.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given a full graph, derive and simplify one compact unit-step expression that matches all intervals.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Convert every segment, combine where possible, and return a concise expression with correct interval behavior.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from single-type segment conversion to full multi-type synthesis and simplification.
solution_step_plan: Convert each segment independently using prior constant/linear patterns.
Sum all windowed terms into one expression.
Group redundant or overlapping terms into a compact form.
Validate expression by testing representative times and all breakpoints.

sections.handoff_notes: Require both exact equivalence and explicit simplification so downstream writers can reuse the final compact form.
